title: The Red Book
author: Carl Gustav Jung
translator: A Folio digest. Jung's Liber Novus (published 2009) is in copyright: these are original summaries, with quotes from his public-domain writings of 1916.
blurb: For sixteen years Jung recorded his own visions in a huge red-leather book, in calligraphy and paintings. Kept secret for a century, it is the map of his journey into the unconscious.

liber novus.m: Latin for 'The New Book' — Jung's title for the Red Book.

visions.m: Images seen in the mind, as in a dream while awake.

vision.m: Images seen in the mind, as in a dream while awake.

unconscious.m: The part of the mind we're not aware of.

individuation.m: Jung's word for becoming your whole, true self.
individuation.e: Therapy helped her individuation — she stopped living others' plans.

mandalas.e: She draws a mandala every morning to calm her mind.

collective.e: Fairy tales live in our collective memory.

cards.title: A secret red book
cards.text: From about 1914 to 1930, Jung copied his inner visions into a large red-leather volume, in gothic calligraphy with his own paintings. He called it Liber Novus, 'The New Book', and kept it private; it was published only in 2009.
cards.quote: we naturally dwell unconsciously in a world of werwolves, demons, magicians
cards.qMean: Deep down, our minds still live among old myths and monsters.
cards.qLife: Why a horror film can scare grown adults who 'know' it's fake.
cards.qBy: C. G. Jung, Collected Papers on Analytical Psychology (1916)
cards.cap: Splendor Solis 21 women washing clothes · public domain

cards.title: Letting the depths speak
cards.text: After his painful break with Freud in 1913, Jung chose to let his fantasies rise freely and wrote down what he saw — floods, blood, voices. He later called this his 'confrontation with the unconscious'.
cards.quote: the soul possesses in some degree historical strata, the oldest stratum of which would correspond to the unconscious.
cards.qMean: The mind has layers; its deepest layer is the unconscious.
cards.qLife: Journalling late at night and surprising yourself with what comes out.
cards.qBy: C. G. Jung, Psychology of the Unconscious (tr. Hinkle, 1916)
cards.cap: Mutus Liber (the Silent Book), 1677 · public domain

cards.title: The mask falls
cards.text: The book opens with Jung realising he had lived for success and the 'spirit of the time'. Another voice — the spirit of the depths — tells him to find his lost soul. The respectable public self, he decides, was only a mask.
cards.quote: a mask which simulates individuality, making others and oneself believe that one is individual, whilst one is only acting a part through which the collective psyche speaks.
cards.qMean: The public mask makes us think we're being ourselves when we're just playing a role.
cards.qLife: Realising your 'dream job' was really your parents' dream.
cards.qBy: C. G. Jung, Collected Papers on Analytical Psychology (1916)

cards.title: Killing the hero
cards.text: In one vision, Jung kills Siegfried, the shining hero. He reads it as the end of his own heroic ideal — the will to conquer everything — so that something deeper can live.
cards.quote: It does not set forth any account of the old events, but rather acts in such a way that it always reveals a thought common to humanity, and once more rejuvenated.
cards.qMean: Myths express shared human ideas again and again.
cards.qLife: Letting go of 'I must win at everything' after burnout.
cards.qBy: C. G. Jung, Psychology of the Unconscious (tr. Hinkle, 1916)
cards.cap: Saint George and the Dragon · public domain

cards.title: Gods and devils within
cards.text: Figures appear and teach him: the prophet Elijah, Salome, and above all Philemon, a wise old man with kingfisher wings. Jung treats them as real voices of the psyche — parts of himself he must listen to.
cards.quote: We have just as much a part in gods and devils, saviours and criminals.
cards.qMean: We all carry both saint and villain inside us.
cards.qLife: Recognising the bully and the kind friend in yourself.
cards.qBy: C. G. Jung, Collected Papers on Analytical Psychology (1916)

cards.title: Becoming whole
cards.text: In the later pages Jung paints circular mandalas. They became, for him, pictures of wholeness — the self uniting its opposites. This process he named individuation, the heart of his later psychology.
cards.quote: leads to individuation beyond the type, and thereby to a new relation to the world and mind.
cards.qMean: Growing past your usual type leads to becoming your whole self.
cards.qLife: A logical person learning to trust feelings, and growing because of it.
cards.qBy: C. G. Jung, Collected Papers on Analytical Psychology (1916)
cards.cap: Four Mandalas, Ngor Monastery, Tibet · public domain
